c.text: Chapter 10 – Growing the Next Leader
The measure nobody uses
Most of us measure our leadership by what is happening now.
Attendance, volunteers on the rota, whether last Sunday went smoothly.
There is a better measure, and it is uncomfortable: what will still be standing five years after you leave, and who will be running it?

By that measure, a leader who builds a thriving ministry that collapses the week he moves away has not really succeeded. And a leader who quietly raises four people who go on to lead has, even if his own numbers were unremarkable.
This is the last chapter because it is the last thing new leaders think about. It should be one of the first.
Paul’s four generations

2 Timothy 2:2 is Paul writing from prison near the end of his life. He tells Timothy to take the things he has heard him say in the presence of many witnesses, and entrust them to faithful people who will be qualified to teach others.
Count the generations in one sentence.
Paul, to Timothy, to faithful people, to others.

Paul is asking Timothy to teach faithfully and to prepare others who can pass that teaching on. The verse looks beyond one gifted teacher to a continuing chain of learning. Timothy, the second person in that chain, was already serving during Paul’s lifetime.
Notice the criterion again: faithful, and able to teach others. Not the most gifted, not the most eager. Reliable, and able to pass it on.
Moses handed over in public, and God told him to

Numbers 27:15-23 records Moses asking God to appoint someone over the community so that the Lord’s people will not be like sheep without a shepherd. He raises the succession question himself, near the end of his life.

God tells him to take Joshua, lay his hand on him, and commission him in the presence of Eleazar the priest and the whole assembly – and to give him some of his own authority so that the whole community will obey him.
Two things to take from this.
The handover was public and explicit. Not a quiet drift where people gradually noticed Joshua doing more. A ceremony, in front of everyone, with authority visibly transferred.
Joshua had been in the room for forty years.

Exodus 24:13 has him going up the mountain with Moses. Exodus 33:11 says that when Moses returned to the camp, his young assistant Joshua did not leave the tent. He had watched Moses meet with God, watched him lead badly-behaved people, watched him fail at Meribah. The commissioning in Numbers 27 was the last step of a very long apprenticeship, not the whole thing.
You cannot produce that in a training course. It comes from letting someone be near you while you work.
Elijah threw his cloak over a man at work
Later in 1 Kings 19:19-21, after the journey to Horeb, Elijah finds Elisha ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen. He throws his cloak around him, signalling a call to follow.
Elisha asks to say goodbye to his parents, then slaughters his oxen, burns the ploughing equipment to cook the meat, gives it to the people, and follows Elijah as his servant.
He burned his own equipment. There was no going back to the farm.

And 2 Kings 2:9-15 shows the completion. Elijah asks what he can do for Elisha before he is taken, and Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit – the inheritance of a firstborn son. After the whirlwind, Elisha picks up the cloak that had fallen and strikes the water with it.
The same cloak. Thrown over him at the plough, picked up at the Jordan.
Ask yourself whose shoulders your cloak is currently on.
Barnabas is the model most of us should copy
If you want one person in Scripture to imitate in this, take Barnabas.

Acts 9:26-27: Saul, newly converted, arrives in Jerusalem and the disciples are all afraid of him, not believing he is really a disciple. Barnabas takes him and brings him to the apostles and vouches for him. Somebody had to stake their reputation on a man everyone distrusted.
Acts 11:25-26: when the church at Antioch grows, Barnabas goes to Tarsus to look for Saul, finds him, and brings him back. He went and fetched him.
Then watch the word order across a few chapters.

In Acts 13:2 the Spirit says to set apart Barnabas and Saul. By Acts 13:13, Luke writes about Paul and his companions. The mentor’s name moves to second place, and Barnabas apparently never makes an issue of it.

And in Acts 15:39 he takes John Mark – the young man who had deserted them – and disappears from the narrative to invest in a failure. That failure, as we saw in Chapter 5, became the man Paul later asked for by name.
Barnabas is not remembered for what he built.
He is remembered for who he made possible.
The thing that actually stops us
Let us be honest about the obstacle, because it is not time and it is not a shortage of people.

It is that raising a successor means admitting you are replaceable. If the young man you train turns out to be better at this than you – more gifted, more liked, more effective – what exactly are you for?
That fear is why leaders keep the interesting work, hand out the tasks, and train nobody. It is rarely conscious. It usually presents itself as high standards.

John 3:30 is John the Baptist’s answer as his own disciples come to him worried that everyone is going to Jesus instead: he must become greater, and I must become less. John says it without bitterness, having just described himself as the friend of the bridegroom who is full of joy at hearing the bridegroom’s voice.

John 14:12 looks ahead to the works Jesus’ followers will do because he is going to the Father. Christians understand the “greater works” in different ways, but the passage is not a claim that a successor becomes greater than Jesus. It directs attention to the continuing work of God through his people.
If someone else’s growth threatens you, bring that honestly to God and to a trusted mentor. Their development is part of the work you have been entrusted with.
How to do it, practically
Spot them by faithfulness.
Look for the person already doing something small, well, without being chased. Availability and teachability matter more than natural talent, and both are visible before you ask.
Bring them into the thinking, not just the doing.

This is the difference between a helper and a leader-in-training. Say out loud why you decided something, including the option you rejected. Let them hear the reasoning, not just receive the conclusion.
Give them something real, early.
Not the chairs – a piece of work with actual decisions attached and their name on it. Use the four steps from Chapter 5.
Allow room to learn in low-risk work.

Agree what they may decide and when they must seek help. An awkward first attempt can teach; avoidable harm cannot be treated as a training exercise. Intervene when safety, safeguarding, money or serious consequences are at stake.
Let them do it differently.
They will. Their way at eighty percent, owned, beats your way at a hundred, borrowed.
Talk about their future, not your vacancy.
Ask what they would like to be doing in three years. Then aim your investment at that, even if it leads out of your ministry.
Hand over in the open.
Numbers 27. When the time comes, say publicly that this person now carries this, and then visibly stop deciding it.
Then get out of the way.
Do not hover, do not take the calls behind their back, and do not let people route around them to you. When someone brings you a question that is now theirs, say so and send them on.
Leaving well
You will not lead this forever. When you go – moved, promoted, retired, or simply finished – leave it better documented, better staffed and better understood than you found it.
Write down how things work.

Introduce your successor personally to the people who matter. Say something publicly and warmly about them. Then leave properly, and resist the temptation to be consulted about everything from a distance.
The most generous thing a departing leader can do is make it clear that the new person has his full confidence – and then stay quiet.
